items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1989-08-13
items.q: Louis, uh, went to work in the same band as Oliver

ctx.x: How did, how did, how did those two meet? How did Oliver and Louis?

Well, uh, Louis, uh, went to work in the same band as Oliver. Uh-huh. Uh, I don't know if it was the Honour or the Tuxedo, but it was one of those. Uh-huh. And so they played together in the band and got to hear each other. Uh-huh. And of course, uh, as it turns out, they were both very much impressed. Uh-huh.
With each other. With each other.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: good jazz people like Oliver and Bunk, you see

ctx.x: That worked certainly. Let's see. We were talking about recording sessions. It was Joe Maera- Mm-hm. He worked with him. Were you working for Joe Maera- Mm-hm.

Not really. What was the basis? No. Let me see what would I say was the basis. Joe, as you know, was very much interested in getting the music of New Orleans recorded. recorded. He has a feeling of commitment about it, the fact that there are a lot of musicians who hadn't been recorded or hadn't been recorded properly. And of course I felt the same way about it, and I always thought of myself as helping out, you know, in many cases proposing and producing sessions myself that I thought were suitable. And so there…
Yeah. Yeah, I'm just wondering how you fit Wiggs into something like this.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: Oliver would signal the break that he was going to make to Louis by fingering the valves on his cornet

ctx.x: Now, those coronet breaks that Louis and Joel did together, they were rehearsed, were they?

No, they weren't rehearsed, but I would say that the principle on which they were done were well-established between them. And the way it worked was that Oliver would signal the break that he was going to make to Louis by fingering the valves on his cornet, and Louis could immediately see what it was that he was going to do. And so when the break came, they would have these miraculous, and there's nothing short of that, two cornet breaks. Of course, jazz fans ever since have appreciated what took place on those…

Now, Al, speaking about the Oliver Band and Louis, how, given the fact that jazz can be defined, or you define jazz as a strict ensemble form in 2-4-4-4 time, with hardly any soloing, how do you explain that someone like Louis, who was born here and played here, ends up changing what I would consider to be the form of jazz to a new form? Although you would say that once the original form was gone, there wasn't a new one to replace it. But let me challenge you with the idea that Louis created a new form for jazz,…
